items.title: Between Two
items.question: Three people stand in a row with A left of B and B left of C. How many people stand between A and C?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 1. With the order A, B, C fixed, only B sits between the two ends.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 1. Placing the three in sequence leaves exactly one person in the middle.
items.lessonContent:
Order constraints fix a single arrangement.
Draw the row before counting.
Middle positions follow from endpoints.
Confirm the order satisfies every clue.

items.title: After Ann
items.question: Ann finishes ahead of Ben, and Ben ahead of Cal. How many runners finish after Ann?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 2. Both Ben and Cal trail Ann in the fixed order.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 2. The chain Ann, Ben, Cal puts two people behind the leader.
items.lessonContent:
Transitive order chains settle ranks.
Count only those behind the target.
Do not confuse ahead with behind.
Verify with the full sequence.

items.title: Shortest of Three
items.question: A is taller than B, and B is taller than C. Who is the shortest?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly C. The chain places C at the bottom of the height order.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is Person C. Following the comparisons downward leads to the last person in the chain.
items.lessonContent:
Transitive relations give a full ranking.
Follow the chain to its end.
One direction fixes the other.
Check the whole order for consistency.

items.title: First and Last
items.question: Four friends line up with D first and A last. How many people stand between them?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 2. With four in line, the two ends leave two people in the middle.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 2. Subtracting the two endpoints from four gives the number in between.
items.lessonContent:
Endpoints reduce the count to inspect.
Subtract fixed positions from the total.
Picture the line before answering.
Check that the middle fits the clues.
Share this: count what lies between two fixed positions in a row.

items.title: All Labels Wrong
items.question: Three boxes are labelled apples, oranges, and mixed, and every label is wrong. What is the fewest boxes you must open to fix all the labels?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 1. Opening the box labelled mixed reveals its true contents and forces the rest.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 1. Because every label is wrong, one well-chosen box determines the other two by elimination.
items.lessonContent:
Wrong information constrains strongly.
One clue can fix the whole system.
Choose the box with the most implications.
Use elimination, not guessing.

items.title: Middle of Five
items.question: Five houses stand in a row, numbered from one end. Which position is the middle house?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 3. Two houses lie on each side of the third.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 3. For an odd row, the middle position is the total plus one, divided by two.
items.lessonContent:
Middle positions follow from odd counts.
Balance the sides around the centre.
Use the formula for odd totals.
Verify by counting both sides.

items.title: Right After
items.question: X stands immediately after Y in a queue, and Y is third. What position does X hold?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 4. Immediately after the third position is the fourth.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 4. Standing directly behind means adding one to the earlier position.
items.lessonContent:
Adjacency shifts a position by one.
Read immediately as the next slot.
Translate words into numbers.
Check the order against the clue.
Share this: convert one relative clue into an exact position.

items.title: Furthest South
items.question: Town X is north of town Y, and town Y is north of town Z. Which town lies furthest south?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly the town named Z. The chain of north-of relations places it below both others.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is Town Z. Reversing the direction from the chain gives the southernmost point.
items.lessonContent:
Direction words create an order.
Follow the chain to its extreme.
One relation implies its reverse.
Sketch before concluding.

items.title: Two Seat Swap
items.question: Four people sit in fixed seats, and two of them swap places. How many people end up in a different seat?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 2. A single swap moves two people and leaves everyone else untouched.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 2. Only the pair exchanging seats changes position; the others stay put.
items.lessonContent:
Track each element's position.
A swap touches exactly two items.
Moves and changes are not the same count.
Verify who actually moved.
Share this: count how many items one exchange displaces.

items.title: One Trip
items.question: Three switches outside a room control three bulbs inside, and you may enter only once. What is the fewest trips into the room needed to match every switch?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 1. Leaving one switch on and warming a second lets heat distinguish the bulbs in a single visit.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 1. Using an extra property beyond on and off lets every switch be identified in one entry.
items.lessonContent:
Add a property to gain information.
Heat, sound, and time can carry signals.
One visit can suffice with clever use of state.
Think beyond binary states.
Share this: solve one identification puzzle by using a second property.

items.title: One Question
items.question: Two guards stand at two doors, one always truthful and one always lying, and you may ask a single question. How many questions do you need to find the safe door?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 1. Asking one guard what the other would say and then taking the opposite door settles it.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 1. A question that routes through both guards cancels the lie and exposes the truth.
items.lessonContent:
Design questions to cancel deception.
Route through both sources at once.
One well-built question beats many.
Think about how lies compose.
Share this: craft one question whose answer is unaffected by whether the source lies.

items.title: Testing a Rule
items.question: A rule claims every card with a vowel on one side has an even number on the other. Which cards must you turn over to test it?
items.correctAnswer: The vowel and the odd number
acceptedAnswers: The vowel and the odd number
the vowel and the odd number
items.correctExplanation: Exactly those two. Only a vowel with an odd number, or an odd with a vowel, can break the rule.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the vowel and the odd number. Cards that cannot violate the rule waste a turn and reveal nothing.
items.lessonContent:
Test a rule by seeking its violation.
Turn only cards that could break it.
Rationalisation wastes effort.
Focus on falsifying cases.
Share this: identify which check would actually disprove one rule.

items.title: Middle of Seven
items.question: Seven people stand in a straight line. Which position is the middle one?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 4. Three people stand on each side of the fourth.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 4. For an odd number, the middle is one more than half the total minus one.
items.lessonContent:
Odd counts have a single centre.
Balance equal numbers on both sides.
Compute the centre directly.
Verify by counting each side.

items.title: Between and Ends
items.question: P stands between Q and R, and Q is at the far left. Who stands at the far right?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly R. With Q leftmost and P in the middle, R must occupy the right end.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is R. Filling the fixed left position and the middle leaves only one slot for the right end.
items.lessonContent:
Fixed ends constrain the middle.
Elimination fills remaining slots.
One known position is often enough.
Place the certain pieces first.

items.title: Empty Seats
items.question: Five seats are arranged in a row, and the second and fourth are occupied. How many seats are empty?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 3. Removing the two occupied seats from five leaves three empty.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 3. Subtract the count of occupied seats from the total to find the remainder.
items.lessonContent:
Partition a total into occupied and empty.
Subtraction answers remainder questions.
List states when the count is small.
Check that the parts sum to the whole.

items.title: Oldest of Three
items.question: Three siblings rank by age: the first is older than the second, who is older than the third. Which sibling is the eldest?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly A. The chain of comparisons places A at the top.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is Person A. Following the age relations upward leads to the first link in the chain.
items.lessonContent:
Transitive comparisons build a ranking.
The chain head is the maximum.
Read direction carefully.
Check the order against every clue.

items.title: Middle Coin
items.question: Three coins lie in a row showing heads, and only the middle one is flipped. How many coins now show tails?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 1. Flipping a single coin changes only that coin.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 1. The unflipped coins keep their original showing.
items.lessonContent:
Track changes to individual items.
A single action affects one element.
Count what changed, not what moved.
Keep the original state in view.

items.title: Sorting Three
items.question: Using a balance that compares two items at a time, what is the maximum number of comparisons needed to sort three objects by weight?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 3. Comparing two, then placing the third in the right slot, can take up to three comparisons.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 3. The worst case is what matters when promising a guaranteed method.
items.lessonContent:
Sorting has a worst case, not just an average.
Plan for the hardest arrangement.
Count comparisons needed to guarantee order.
Promises must hold in every case.

items.title: Not First Not Last
items.question: Among three runners, A is not first and B is not last. Which person must finish in the middle?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly A. Since A is not first in a field of three, A occupies either second or third, and the other clue forces the middle.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is Runner A. Combining both exclusions leaves only the middle position open.
items.lessonContent:
Exclusions narrow possibilities.
Combine constraints, not just one.
Eliminate until a single option remains.
Test candidates against every clue.

items.title: Ends Fixed
items.question: Four rooms line a corridor with the kitchen at one end and the bedroom at the other. How many rooms lie between them?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 2. With four rooms and two ends occupied, two remain in the middle.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 2. Subtract the two fixed end rooms from the total to get those between.
items.lessonContent:
Fixed endpoints leave a fixed middle.
Subtract the ends from the total.
Picture the line to confirm.
Check the remainder fits the clues.

items.title: Three Days On
items.question: If today is Wednesday, what day of the week is it three days later?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly Saturday. Counting forward three days from Wednesday lands on Saturday.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is Saturday. Walking the days one at a time avoids off-by-one slips.
items.lessonContent:
Cycles repeat in fixed steps.
Advance one unit at a time for safety.
Watch for inclusive counting errors.
Verify by counting on your fingers.

items.title: Passing Ball
items.question: Five friends in a circle pass a ball to the next person each time. Starting at person one, who holds it after four passes?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly person five. Four passes move the ball four positions around the circle.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 5. Counting each pass one step at a time gives the holder directly.
items.lessonContent:
Discrete motion counts in steps.
Track each handover in order.
Modular arithmetic wraps around.
Count slowly to avoid skipping.

items.title: Mixed Box
items.question: Three boxes are labelled apples, oranges, and mixed, and every label is wrong. Which one box reveals the rest when opened?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly the mixed box. Since it cannot be mixed, it must be a single fruit, which forces the other two.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is the mixed box. Opening a single-fruit box leaves an ambiguity that the mixed label resolves.
items.lessonContent:
Choose the clue with the strongest implications.
A necessarily-wrong label is a gift.
Elimination resolves the remaining cases.
Open the box that spreads information.

items.title: Queue Count
items.question: Sam is third from the front and second from the back of a queue. How many people are in the queue?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly 4. Two people stand ahead and one behind, giving four in total.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 4. Adding the front count, the back count, and Sam gives the total.
items.lessonContent:
Positions from both ends overlap.
Add the two counts and subtract the overlap.
Draw the queue to confirm.
Watch for double-counting.

items.title: Not Enough Clues
items.question: In a row of five people, the tallest is first and the shortest is fifth. Who is third?
items.correctExplanation: It cannot be determined. The two extremes say nothing about the order of the middle three.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is cannot be determined. Underspecified puzzles have several valid arrangements, so no unique answer exists.
items.lessonContent:
Recognise when clues are insufficient.
Several solutions may fit the same facts.
Do not invent extra constraints.
Say what cannot be known.
